title: Clinical Roadmap: Sudden vs. Gradual Vision Loss
summary: An exhaustive diagnostic framework for Ophthalmic assessment, categorizing vision loss by onset (sudden vs. gradual), presence of pain, duration, and anatomical findings. This guide ensures high-fidelity clinical differentiation across all major ocular pathologies.

branches: Few seconds’ duration (Unilateral): GCA (age >55y, weight loss, fatigue, jaw/tongue claudication, pulseless/tender/thickened temporal artery, ieSr/Crp); Papilloedema (bilateral disc swelling, loss of SVp, peripapillary haemorrhages, features of raised ICp); Impending CRVO (dilated, tortuous retinal veins, haemorrhages); OIS (veins dilated and irregular but not tortuous, mid-peripheral haemorrhages; ± NVD, iIOp, carotid bruits).
Few seconds’ duration (Bilateral): Papilloedema: see described previously.
Few minutes’ duration (Unilateral): Amaurosis fugax (complete or partial monocular blindness ± evidence of emboli, AF, carotid bruits); GCA (see described previously).
Few minutes’ duration (Bilateral): Vertebrobasilar artery insufficiency (recurrent episodes ± ataxia, dysphasia, dysarthria, hemiparesis, hemisensory disturbance).

Up to 1h duration (Bilateral): Migraine: aura—fortification spectra, transient VF defects; followed by unilateral headache, associated nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonopohobia, exercise aggravation, and often FH.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Cornea & Vitreous
content: Abnormal cornea - Hydrops: acute corneal oedema associated with underlying disease such as keratoconus.
Abnormal vitreous - Vitreous haemorrhage: varies from microscopic level to completely obscuring the fundus.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Abnormal Fundus (Vascular & Retinal)

rows: rApD, attenuated arterioles, pale fundus, cherry-red spot.
dilated tortuous veins, haemorrhages in all four quadrants ± macular oedema ± CWS, rApD; BrVO may give symptomatic altitudinal defects, particularly if on temporal arcade.
flashes/floaters, tobacco dust, convex elevated retina with (multiple) break(s).
convex elevated retina with shifting fluid, no break.
concave elevated retina with tractional membranes.
floaters, vitritis, snow balls/banking ± macular oedema.
floaters, significantly reduced vision; vitritis, retinal/ choroidal infiltrates, macular oedema, vascular sheathing/occlusion, haemorrhages.

sections.title: Persistent Painless Loss: Disc, Macula & Normal Fundus
content: Abnormal disc - AION: rApD, pale oedematous disc ± flame-shaped haemorrhages; may have altitudinal field defect; may be arteritic (with symptoms of GCA) or non-arteritic (usually sectoral disc swelling).
Abnormal macula - Choroidal neovascular membrane: distortion ± positive scotoma, drusen, subretinal membrane ± haemorrhage, exudate.
Abnormal macula - CSC: colour desaturation, micropsia, serous detachment of neurosensory retina.
Normal fundus - Cortical blindness: ± denial, small residual field; normal pupil reactions; abnormal CT/MrI head.

Normal fundus - Functional: inconsistent acuity between different tests and at different times, normal ophthalmic examination, normal eDTs, spiralling and/or crossing of isopters on kinetic perimetry.

sections.title: Sudden/Recent Loss of Vision: Painful
content: Abnormal cornea - APAC: usually hypermetropic, haloes, frontal headache, vomiting; injected, corneal oedema, fixed semi-dilated pupil, shallow AC with closed angle, raised IOp.
Abnormal cornea - Bullous keratopathy: thickened, hazy cornea, stromal/subepithelial oedema, bullae, evidence of underlying pathology, e.g. ACIOl, Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy, etc.
Abnormal cornea - Keratitis: photophobia, watering, circumlimbal injection, corneal infiltrate ± epithelial defect ± AC activity.

Abnormal disc - Optic neuritis: usually age 18–45y, with retro-orbital pain, especially on eye movement, rApD, reduced colour vision, VF defects, swollen disc ± peripapillary flame-shaped haemorrhages; may also be painless.
Abnormal uvea - Anterior uveitis: anterior pain, photophobia, mildly reduced vision, circumlimbal injection, AC cells and flare, Kps.
Normal fundus - Retrobulbar neuritis: as for optic neuritis, but with a normal disc; may also be painless.

sections.title: Gradual Loss of Vision: Generalized
content: Abnormal cornea - Corneal dystrophies: corneal clouding (deposition/oedema); usually bilateral but may be asymmetric; common types include Fuchs’ endothelial dystrophy in the elderly and reis–Bucklers dystrophy in young adults.
Abnormal cornea - Keratoconus: refractive error from progressive astigmatism; corneal oedema from acute hydrops; usually bilateral but may be asymmetric.
Abnormal lens - Cataract: uni- or bilateral opacification of the lens; cloudy, misty; glare; commonest in the elderly.

sections.title: Gradual Loss of Vision: Central (Macula)
content: Note: Macular disease usually leads to distortion ± micropsia and early dVA; pupillary responses and colour vision are relatively preserved.
AMD: very common bilateral disease of the elderly; the commonest type is ‘dry’ changes which are associated with gradual, patchy central loss.
Macular dystrophies: group of diseases with specific patterns occurring in younger age group; bilateral disease; may have FH, and genetic testing is sometimes possible.
Diabetic maculopathy: ischaemia may lead to gradual dVA; oedema may lead to more acute distortion/dVA; associated with other diabetic changes.
CMO: oedema resulting in distortion/dVA; may be associated with surgery, inflammation, or vascular disease.

sections.title: Gradual Loss: Central (Optic Disc/Nerve)
content: Note: Optic nerve disease usually leads to dimness and darkening of colours; although commonly central, it may lead to peripheral or generalized loss of vision; pupillary responses, colour vision, and brightness testing are all reduced.
Compressive optic neuropathy: progressive dVA, disc pallor ± pain, involvement of other local structures.
LHON: severe sequential dVA over weeks/months, telangiectatic vessels around disc (acutely); usually young adult ♂; FH.
Toxic or nutritional optic neuropathies: slowly progressive, symmetrical dVA with central scotomata; relevant nutritional, therapeutic, or toxic history.
Inflammatory optic neuropathies: associated with systemic disease (e.g. sarcoid, vasculitis, and syphilis); often very steroid-sensitive.
Chronic papilloedema: sustained disc swelling due to raised ICp may cause permanent optic nerve dysfunction, including dVA and field defects, and optic disc pallor.

sections.title: Gradual Loss: Peripheral or Patchy
content: Abnormal choroid/retina - Posterior uveitis: floaters, patchy loss of vision ± central distortion/dVA from CMO; may include chorioretinitis, vitritis, and retinal vasculitis.
Abnormal choroid/retina - RP: bilateral concentric field loss, peripheral ‘bone spicule’ pigmentation, retinal arteriole attenuation, and optic disc pallor.
Abnormal optic disc - Glaucoma: asymptomatic peripheral field loss; usually bilateral, but often asymmetric; characteristic cupping and other disc changes; often associated with iIOp.
